title: Frequently Asked Questions
subtitle: The SWIRL mixing protocol — what it guarantees, what it does not, and how to verify both.
s1a1: SWIRL is a mixing layer for Lightning payments. It receives deposits over static BOLT12 offers, pools them into a continuously deepening anonymity set, and pays out in uniform denominations on randomized schedules — with an optional submarine-swap exit to layer 1. The goal is narrow and measurable: a settlement that arrives at your wallet cannot be linked to the payment that entered the pool.
s1a2: The pool holds funds only while a mix is in flight — never as a balance, never tied to an identity. There is no account system, and no operator wallet that can redirect your sats anywhere but your own authorized exit. Your claim is the receipt credential issued at deposit: lose it, and no one — including us — can recover the exit for you.
s1a3: The pool never closes. Deposits accumulate continuously behind unannounced channels; every payout is decomposed into standard denomination chunks, shuffled against all live deposits, and released through a randomized delay queue after a minimum hold. The anonymity set is the pool's live depth — every depositor your funds are indistinguishable among — not a fixed batch that empties and resets.
s1q4: Does it run on mainnet today?
s1a4: The engine is functional and covered by an end-to-end regtest suite; public infrastructure currently runs against testnet-class parameters while the audit surface is completed. Mainnet parameters ship with the source release. The DAPP page shows live pool state as that infrastructure comes online.
s2q1: What does an outside observer actually see?
s2a1: A payer sees a one-time invoice ending in a blinded path. A relay sees one hop of an onion. The public graph sees nothing — pool channels are unannounced. A chain analyst watching a loop-out sees a swap output shared with thousands of unrelated users. Each observer gets a fragment; no observer can assemble the flow.
s2a2: Three independent randomization layers: every exit is shuffled against the pool's full live depth; each chunk waits its own uniformly drawn delay between configurable bounds; and a minimum hold, counted from your deposit and invisible to observers, gates every payout. Order, rhythm, and timing are all decorrelated from deposits.
s2q3: How strong is the anonymity, formally?
s2a3: Bounded by live depth, and we say so. With N deposits live in the pool, an observer's residual information is log₂(N) bits — participation, and nothing else. A deeper pool means strictly more plausible deniability per chunk. This is why the pool is designed to never close and only grow — depth compounds instead of resetting.
s2q4: Can the coordinator link my deposit to my payout?
s2a4: While a settlement is in flight, the coordinator necessarily sees both sides — that is the honest limit of any non-cryptographic pool. The mitigation is structural: state lives in memory only, job records purge on a retention window measured in hours, and there is no account layer to accumulate history. After settlement, the transcript is gone.
s3a1: A static, reusable payment code (lno1…) that never expires and never names your node. Payers use it to negotiate a fresh, single-use invoice over Lightning's onion-messaging layer. You publish it once and receive forever — no per-customer invoices, no web server, no database of payers.
s3q2: How is this different from a Lightning address or LNURL?
s3a2: LNURL moves invoice negotiation to HTTPS, which inserts a web server into your privacy model: it learns your node, your payers, and their IP addresses, and it can be seized or subpoenaed. BOLT12 keeps negotiation inside onion-routed Lightning messages. There is no server in the loop because the protocol does not need one.
s3q3: Do I need public channels to receive?
s3a3: No — the opposite. SWIRL nodes run behind unannounced channels only, so the network never learns your channel graph. Every generated invoice terminates in a blinded path whose final hops are single-use pseudonyms. Public channels would defeat the purpose; the protocol is built around their absence.
s4q1: Why are payouts cut into standard amounts?
s4a1: Because a unique amount is a fingerprint. If 0.0187334 BTC goes in and 0.0187334 BTC comes out, no shuffle unlinks them. Cutting every payout from a fixed lattice (0.001 / 0.01 / 0.1 / 1 BTC) makes every chunk indistinguishable from every other chunk of its size — and makes subset-sum analysis underdetermined by construction.
s4q2: What happens to the remainder that doesn't fit the lattice?
s4a2: It is never paid out as itself — that would reintroduce a unique amount. Residuals are carried forward and re-enter the pool as fresh deposits, where they merge with other funds before being cut again.
s4q3: Is there a minimum mix amount?
s4a3: The practical floor is one lattice quantum — currently 0.001 BTC. Below that there is no standard denomination to hide inside. Larger amounts simply decompose into more chunks across more tiers; there is no protocol-level ceiling.
s5q1: How long does a mix take?
s5a1: With defaults: a minimum hold of 30 minutes after your deposit enters the pool, then each chunk joins the exit queue and releases with up to 60 minutes of independent random delay. A typical five-chunk payout completes within a couple of hours. Privacy-bearing delay is a feature of the design, not a performance bug.
s5a2: Every timing parameter is operator-tunable (min-hold, exit-jitter-max, min/max-delay). Shorter holds and tighter delays settle sooner and unlink less. The knobs are yours; the trade-off is explicit, and the defaults are conservative on purpose.
s5q3: Is there ever too little liquidity to mix?
s5a3: There is no quorum to reach and no batch to wait for — the pool settles continuously and its depth only grows with deposits. The status output always shows the live depth you are mixing against, so you see exactly what anonymity you got rather than pretending the crowd was bigger.
s6q1: How do funds move from Lightning to layer 1?
s6a1: Through a submarine swap: your node pays an off-chain HTLC locked to a preimage hash, the swap provider pays an on-chain output locked to the same hash, and the preimage settles both legs at once. The output address is fresh for every swap and its only on-chain relationship is to the provider — a utility shared with thousands of users.
s6a2: Atomic, which is the property that matters: either both legs execute or both unwind at expiry. Neither side can walk away with the other's funds mid-swap. Note that atomicity is not anonymity — the swap composes with the deep pool and jitter; it does not replace them.
s6a3: The module ships behind the swirl-loopout-enabled flag, default off, while the provider-integration surface is hardened against fee griefing and probing. With the flag off, exits settle over Lightning only and no on-chain footprint is created at all.
s7a1: You do. The console never asks for keys or seed phrases — ever. While a mix is in flight, funds sit inside the pool under its settlement constructions, and the only claim on the exit is your receipt credential, encrypted on your own device under a phrase we never see.
s7q2: What logs exist, and for how long?
s7a2: Pool state is memory-only and dies with the process. Job records persist for a configurable retention window (default 24 hours) solely so you can inspect settlement, then purge. A minimal-logs flag strips sensitive fields from operational output. There is no analytics, no telemetry, and no database to breach.
s7q3: Should I run my node over Tor?
s7a3: Yes. Network-layer metadata is outside the protocol's scope: if your node answers on an IP address tied to your identity, routing cryptography cannot help you. Tor support is the documented deployment posture, and the reference stack binds no clearnet interface.
s7a4: Three, stated plainly: the coordinator sees both sides while a settlement is in flight; a shallow pool is a small anonymity set no matter how good the shuffle is; and endpoint hygiene — your IP, your wallet fingerprints, your reuse of infrastructure — remains your responsibility. SWIRL is one layer in a stack, engineered to never be the weak one.
s8q1: Can I verify these claims myself?
s8a1: Yes — that is the point of the regtest harness. A Docker Compose stack boots isolated CLN nodes, opens unannounced channels, and drives full mix jobs end to end, asserting per settlement: no amount matches, no order correlation, delays within bounds, and no node identity in any deposit transcript. The raw transcripts are printed, not summarized.
s8a2: The harness and reference configuration ship with the mainnet parameter release. Until then, the CLI surface is documented in full on this site, and the DAPP page renders live pool state from the same schema the harness emits — the public transcript is the audit trail.
s8a3: Three RPC methods on your own node — swirl-offer, swirl-mix, swirl-status — plus twelve node options covering fees, minimum hold, delays, jitter, retention, and the loop-out flag. No REST gateway, no keys in the cloud, no third party in the call path. See Docs → CLI Reference.
s9a1: SWIRL is the governance asset of the pool: a fixed supply of 21,000,000 issued as an RGB-20 token, client-side validated and committed into Taproot outputs. The allocation: 5% early-user airdrop, 10% anonymity mining, 55% DAO treasury, 30% founders and early backers — minted once at genesis, no inflation ever. It has one job: governing the pool. It is not a payment token and not a claim on pool funds.
s9a2: Voting power is locked SWIRL and nothing else. Lock more, weigh more; unlock only after a governance-set cooldown. Delegation is first-class — you can assign your weight to an operator and undelegate in a single transaction. Creating a proposal requires at least 2,100 SWIRL locked.
s9a3: The parameters that define the pool: the denomination fee schedule, the minimum hold time, new denomination lanes, the cross-chain gateway set, and the treasury split between liquidity incentives, mining rebates and reserve. Passed proposals execute after a timelock, so anyone who disagrees has time to exit first.
s9a4: No. SWIRL issuance is planned, not live — everything in the console's governance tab is marked SOON. Any 'SWIRL' trading anywhere today is not us. Early liquidity earns weight through anonymity mining, and that weight maps into an allocation when the token launches.
